page_title: Here’s Why Juicero’s Press is So Expensive

sources.entry: A good example of over-engineering: the Juicero press (April 2017)

summary.title: Here's Why Juicero's Press is So Expensive
summary.one_liner: A teardown of the Juicero press that argues its cost came from unconstrained hardware development: heavy machined aluminum, custom power supply and gearbox, and a squeeze-force design that a human hand does more simply.
takeaways: Juicero's press used roughly eight machined aluminum parts and a complex gearbox, which the author believes made machined parts over half the BOM cost.
Early constraints push hardware founders to find cheaper, creative solutions; spending heavily before shipping a unit tests assumptions too late.
The press's core design choice was applying force across the whole ~64 sq in pack at once, while a hand squeezes a smaller area, which the author argues could have saved hundreds of dollars.
Even simple features like door locking used many parts (10 custom molded parts, a solenoid, springs, bushings), an example of unnecessary complexity.
The author suggests a lean approach (e.g., per-pack pricing instead of a fixed weekly subscription) could have produced a more viable product.
summary.summary: The author, a co-founder of the hardware investor Bolt, takes apart the Juicero press after a Bloomberg article showed the juice packs could be squeezed by hand. The post describes the press's complex internals: injection-molded shells, machined aluminum structure, a custom high-voltage power supply, a CC3200 WiFi chip and STM32 processor, a gearbox, and a locking mechanism with many parts. It then ties the cost to the design decision to press the whole pack at once, and to the company spending about $120M over two years before shipping. The argument is a lesson for hardware startups: test core assumptions with customers early and iterate instead of over-engineering.
